cc-cfg-permissions.why: Safety + convenience: routine without confirmation, dangerous — never.
cc-cfg-permissions.when: Every time you notice repeated confirmations — you need an allow rule.
cc-cfg-permissions.impact: Workflow instead of constant "confirm Y/n" on every command.
cc-cfg-permissions.example: deny: [Bash(rm -rf:*), Edit(./package.json)] — critical actions are hard-blocked.
cc-cfg-permissions.mistakes: Rules too broad like allow: [Bash(*)] — you lose control over what's executed.

cc-cfg-statusline.title: Statusline
cc-cfg-statusline.what: A custom terminal bottom line — shows context: git branch, model, tokens, your markers.
cc-cfg-statusline.why: So you see the session state without running commands — branch / model / context limit.
cc-cfg-statusline.when: When you work on several projects in parallel — you need an anchor.
cc-cfg-statusline.impact: Fewer switches, fewer mistakes like "committed to the wrong branch".
cc-cfg-statusline.example: statusLine.command — a shell command that returns the status line. Cached for ~300ms.
cc-cfg-statusline.mistakes: A heavy shell script in Statusline — slows every edit.

cc-slash.title: Slash commands
cc-slash.what: Commands like [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]], [[node:cc-cmd-clear|/clear]], [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]], /model, /review — built-in and custom. Work in both the terminal and [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] chats.
cc-slash.why: Launch complex scenarios with a single press — without a long prompt.
cc-slash.when: When the task is typical: review, init, context cleanup, model switch.
cc-slash.impact: Instead of typing "help me rename the conversation and compact the history" — three chars `/r`, then autocomplete, then Enter. Time saved per session: 15-20 minutes.
cc-slash.example: /review — structured code review of the current branch. [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]] — compress context without losing history.
cc-slash.mistakes: Ignoring [[node:cc-cmd-clear|/clear]] when context goes "stale" — answer quality drops.

cc-cmd-init.title: /init — initialize
cc-cmd-init.what: Scans the current project and generates [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: stack, conventions, entry points, taboos.
cc-cmd-init.why: So you don't write [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] from scratch — the model describes the frame, you fine-tune.
cc-cmd-init.when: On the first [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] launch in a new project.
cc-cmd-init.impact: 30 minutes of manual work becomes 3 minutes, plus coverage of what you wouldn't have thought of.
cc-cmd-init.example: claude in the repo, then /init, then finalize the "taboos" and "architectural decisions" sections.
cc-cmd-init.mistakes: Using the generated file as final — without edits it's bloated.

cc-cmd-clear.title: /clear — clear chat
cc-cmd-clear.what: Clears the current conversation and context — starts a new chat with the same [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] and Hooks.
cc-cmd-clear.why: To free the [[node:b-context|context window]] when a task is closed or the topic changed.
cc-cmd-clear.when: After finishing a subtask, before starting another large piece of work.
cc-cmd-clear.impact: On a fresh context Claude answers accurately on the first try. On a loaded one — gets confused with old details, you spend 2-3 iterations clarifying. Simple rule: new task — /clear.
cc-cmd-clear.example: /clear after a PR review, before refactoring another part of the code.
cc-cmd-clear.mistakes: Doing /clear mid-work and losing intermediate conclusions — [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]] is better.

cc-cmd-compact.title: /compact — compress context
cc-cmd-compact.what: Compresses the current context — the model summarizes history and continues with a compact version.
cc-cmd-compact.why: [[node:b-context|Context window]] close to the limit, but you can't lose history — the task is in progress.
cc-cmd-compact.when: When the chat has grown and the model has begun "forgetting" details of earlier discussions.
cc-cmd-compact.impact: Frees 80-90% of context while preserving key conclusions.
cc-cmd-compact.example: /compact after long research, before moving to writing code.
cc-cmd-compact.mistakes: Relying on compact forever — sooner or later a full [[node:cc-cmd-clear|/clear]] is needed.

cc-cmd-model.title: /model — pick model
cc-cmd-model.what: Switches the current session's model — Opus / Sonnet / Haiku — without restart.
cc-cmd-model.why: Different tasks — different models: research on Opus, generation on Sonnet, routine on Haiku.
cc-cmd-model.when: When the task requires different depth or speed than the starting model.
cc-cmd-model.impact: The right model = either 5× faster or 2× deeper.
cc-cmd-model.example: /model sonnet for routine, then /model opus for an architectural decision, then back.
cc-cmd-model.mistakes: Doing everything on one model — either slow/expensive or shallow.

cc-cmd-permissions.title: /permissions — Permissions
cc-cmd-permissions.what: Interactive permissions management — what Claude can do without confirmation.
cc-cmd-permissions.why: So you don't confirm every Bash/Edit by hand, but block the destructive.
cc-cmd-permissions.when: On initial project setup and when adding new command types.
cc-cmd-permissions.impact: 80% of confirmations go away — safe actions run automatically.
cc-cmd-permissions.example: /permissions, then allow Bash(npm test) and Edit(./src/**), deny Bash(rm -rf:*).
cc-cmd-permissions.mistakes: Allowing everything — you lose control over what changes.

cc-cmd-agents.title: /agents — manage
cc-cmd-agents.what: List and configure Subagents: which are available, descriptions, creating new ones.
cc-cmd-agents.why: So you see which agents Claude can call and quickly create new ones.
cc-cmd-agents.when: When configuring hidden processes and debugging why an agent isn't activating.
cc-cmd-agents.impact: Transparency about what Claude can delegate without your involvement.
cc-cmd-agents.example: /agents, then create code-reviewer with the trigger "review PR", description and steps.
cc-cmd-agents.mistakes: Creating an agent without a clear trigger in description — it'll never activate.

cc-cmd-mcp.title: /mcp — MCP servers
cc-cmd-mcp.what: Manage MCP servers: list connected ones, add new, debug.
cc-cmd-mcp.why: So you see what Claude has access to from external systems (tracker, docs, DB).
cc-cmd-mcp.when: On connecting a new integration and on errors like "can't see the data".
cc-cmd-mcp.impact: Access transparency: clear what Claude can read and change outside.
cc-cmd-mcp.example: /mcp, then add a server with a token, then check that the exposed tools are available.
cc-cmd-mcp.mistakes: Connecting everything in a row — each server loads at startup, slowing it down.

cc-cmd-review.title: /review — code review
cc-cmd-review.what: Runs a specialized code review of the current branch or the specified PR.
cc-cmd-review.why: A structured audit instead of "take a look" — with priority and rationale.
cc-cmd-review.when: Before merge, after a large edit, on suspicion of regression.
cc-cmd-review.impact: Review quality at the level of an experienced developer, time — minutes instead of an hour.
cc-cmd-review.example: /review without arguments on the current branch, then report with categories "critical / important / optional".
cc-cmd-review.mistakes: Relying only on /review without a human eye — doesn't replace architectural thinking.

cc-cmd-custom.title: Custom slash commands
cc-cmd-custom.what: Your own / commands in .claude/commands/<name>.md — markdown with Claude instructions.
cc-cmd-custom.why: To turn a recurring long prompt into one short command.
cc-cmd-custom.when: If you repeat the same complex request ≥ 3 times.
cc-cmd-custom.impact: One press instead of 300 characters of prompt — multiplies the speed of recurring routine.
cc-cmd-custom.example: .claude/commands/dev-task.md, then now /dev-task in chat runs your template.
cc-cmd-custom.mistakes: Making a command for a one-off task — no payoff.

cc-hooks.title: Hooks
cc-hooks.what: Hooks in settings.json: shell commands executed on events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop and others).
cc-hooks.why: Behavior automation: "after every Write — run the linter", "before Bash — check the command".
cc-hooks.when: When you need a guaranteed action on an event, without reminding the model.
cc-hooks.impact: Hooks turn [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] from an assistant into a disciplined junior.
cc-hooks.mistakes: Without Hooks, hoping the model "won't forget" to format — it will forget.

cc-md.title: CLAUDE.md
cc-md.what: A [[node:p-instructions|project instructions]] file: stack, conventions, important paths, taboos. Loaded into every conversation.
cc-md.why: It's the project's "character" in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — like [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] but for code.
cc-md.when: In every project that uses [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — mandatory.
cc-md.impact: Without CLAUDE.md the model spends the first 10 minutes on what's already described.
cc-md.example: Generate CLAUDE.md via [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] and add "don't use any in TypeScript".
cc-md.mistakes: Listing the obvious there (repo name, that it's React) — rules and taboos are more valuable.

cc-subagents.title: Subagents
cc-subagents.what: Parallel agents inside [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]: Explore (search), Plan (planning), general-purpose.
cc-subagents.why: They take on the "dirty" work — context isolation of the parent agent.
cc-subagents.when: On large research, long searches, parallel tasks.
cc-subagents.impact: Subagents save the main context and speed up the task 2-4×.
cc-subagents.example: Run an Explore agent to find all places where the deprecated API is used.
cc-subagents.mistakes: Doing all tasks in the main chat — you overflow the context and lose focus.

cc-plan-mode.title: Plan Mode
cc-plan-mode.what: A special [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] mode: the model builds a change plan as a structured list but does NOT apply edits. You review the plan, approve — and only then execution proceeds.
cc-plan-mode.why: Plan mode protects against "oops" on big edits: you see all the steps before they touch files. Especially valuable on legacy and architectural refactors.
cc-plan-mode.when: Before mass changes (10+ files), before migrations, before edits in sensitive places (auth, payments, DB migrations).
cc-plan-mode.impact: On big edits: 5 minutes reviewing the plan = an hour saved on rollback when AI goes off-track. Without a plan: one in five runs needs to be redone from scratch.
cc-plan-mode.example: In chat: "Enter plan mode and propose a refactor plan for this module. No edits until my OK".
cc-plan-mode.mistakes: Using Plan mode on trivial edits (one line, one file) — overhead without benefit. Plan — for dangerous and large steps.

cc-ide.title: IDE extensions
cc-ide.what: [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] in VS Code and JetBrains: same agent, but with inline edits right in the editor, a diff view with accept/reject, sync with open tabs. Installed from marketplace.
cc-ide.why: So you don't switch between terminal and IDE on every edit: fewer context switches, faster review of changes.
cc-ide.when: When the main work is in the IDE and Claude needs to be "at hand" inside the editor, not in a separate terminal window.
cc-ide.impact: IDE integration = 1.5-2× faster accept/reject cycle vs the terminal; you see the edit in the surrounding code context.
cc-ide.example: Install the VS Code extension, then Cmd+Shift+P, then Claude: ask in current file, and the edit arrives as an inline diff.
cc-ide.mistakes: Using only the IDE extension and not knowing the CLI — you lose sessions, --resume, plugins. They complement each other, not replace.

mcp.title: MCP
mcp.what: Model Context Protocol — a standard for connecting external tools and data to Claude (like "USB-C" for AI).
mcp.why: So Claude sees Linear, Jira, Figma, DBs, files — without copy-paste and manual API wiring.
mcp.when: When Claude needs to "live" in your environment: know tickets, read designs, run queries.
mcp.impact: MCP is the difference between "AI chat" and "AI coworker who has access to work tools".
mcp.example: Connect MCP Linear, then ask "take all P0 bugs from the sprint and group them by component".
mcp.mistakes: Giving an MCP server too many privileges — a potential data leak.

m-what.title: What MCP is
m-what.what: An open protocol: the server exposes tools/resources, the client (Claude) calls them.
m-what.why: Once and for all standardizes the connection — before, every product invented its own plugin API.
m-what.when: When you want to give Claude access to a new system: API, DB, repo, task board.
m-what.impact: One protocol instead of dozens of integrations — the ecosystem grows fast.
m-what.example: Explain how MCP differs from a regular API integrator and why it matters.
m-what.mistakes: Confusing MCP with REST API — it's a different layer: orchestrating model tools, not requests.

m-ready.title: Ready-made MCP servers
m-ready.what:
Ready-made MCP servers are found in two places today:

- **The official MCP Registry** — registry.modelcontextprotocol.io: a catalog of thousands of servers (on the order of 10,000 public ones), with metadata pointing to npm/PyPI/Docker. The old GitHub catalog `modelcontextprotocol/servers` was cut down to ~7 reference servers (Fetch, Filesystem, Git, Memory and others); the rest moved to an archive.
- **The Connectors directory in Claude** (Settings → Connectors) — Anthropic-verified and vendor-built **remote connectors** with OAuth: Notion, Figma, Stripe, PayPal, Linear, Slack, GitHub, Canva, Microsoft 365 and dozens more. Available on all plans, including Free.

Local stdio servers (file system, your own scripts) remain a separate mechanism in Claude Desktop / Claude Code.

The protocol itself has lived in the **Agentic AI Foundation** (Linux Foundation) since December 2025 and is adopted well beyond Anthropic: ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot.

*As of this writing (2026-08) — the registry and the connectors directory keep growing; check there.*
m-ready.why: Enable one connector — get dozens of ready tools with authentication, schemas and error handling already worked out. Your own connector = 1-4 weeks of development plus permanent maintenance. And MCP becoming an industry-wide standard means one server works from Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and IDEs at once.
m-ready.when: If the product is already in the catalog — take the ready one (for popular services that's almost always the case). Write your own only if: (a) the service isn't in the registry, (b) you need specific server-side logic, (c) compliance forbids third-party servers.
m-ready.impact: A ready connector: minutes to hook up via OAuth vs weeks to build your own. Plus updates arrive automatically when the vendor changes their API.
m-ready.example: "I want Claude to read Linear tickets and open PRs in GitHub." Solution: Settings → Connectors → connect Linear and GitHub via OAuth — no config files. Working in 5 minutes. The local route (your own scripts, files) is still via Claude Desktop / Claude Code config.
m-ready.mistakes:
❌ Writing your own connector to Jira/Slack/Figma — the official one covers 95% of tasks.
❌ Attaching a community server to a production environment without a code audit — a security risk.
❌ Not checking scopes/permissions during the OAuth connection — you give Claude more rights than needed.
❌ Ignoring the **MCP Inspector** when debugging your own servers — hours lost guessing at errors.

*deprecate-watch: the catalogs grow monthly; the structure (registry + connectors directory + local stdio) is as of 2026-08.*

m-custom.title: Your own MCP server
m-custom.what: Written in TypeScript/Python via the Anthropic SDK. You declare tools and resources — the client sees them.
m-custom.why: To give Claude access to an internal system that isn't in the public catalog.
m-custom.when: When the company has its own CRM, BI, DB wrapper — and no ready-made MCP for it.
m-custom.impact: Your own server = the only way to connect a unique internal tool.
m-custom.example: Make an MCP server with a get_active_users(period) tool against our PostgreSQL.
m-custom.mistakes: Opening too many tools at once — Claude gets confused about what to pick.

m-security.title: Security
m-security.what: An MCP server runs locally or remotely — it sees exactly what you gave it (tokens, keys).
m-security.why: Principle of least privilege: read-only for analytics, write only where required.
m-security.when: Before connecting any MCP — especially unofficial ones.
m-security.impact: Minimum privileges = minimum blast radius on error or compromise.
m-security.example: Connect Linear MCP in read-only mode — let it only read tickets, not edit.
m-security.mistakes: Running an unknown MCP server with full privileges — that's executing someone else's code.

m-patterns.title: Design patterns
m-patterns.what: Best practices for MCP server design: minimal tools surface, meaningful namespace, explicit side-effect description, idempotency, separation of read and write.
m-patterns.why: So Claude picks tools correctly and doesn't pull the wrong ones; for long-term operation without surprises.
m-patterns.when: When designing any custom MCP server, especially for a team or client.
m-patterns.impact: Good patterns = 3-5× fewer tool-choice errors from Claude.
m-patterns.example: Split into get_users (read) and delete_user (write+confirm). Not one super_users(action) — Claude will get the namespace confused.
m-patterns.mistakes: Making a "universal tool" with ten parameters — Claude gets lost. Better 3 narrow tools than one broad one.

m-debug.title: MCP debugging
m-debug.what: The /mcp command in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] shows: which servers are connected, which tools are visible, which errors. Server logs + detailed request output help understand "why it doesn't work".
m-debug.why: Without debugging, "MCP doesn't see my data" stays forever. A systematic approach saves hours.
m-debug.when: When a new server is connected but Claude "doesn't use it" or calls it with wrong parameters.
m-debug.impact: Knowing /mcp + logs = fixing the problem in 5-10 minutes instead of random attempts.
m-debug.example: /mcp, then check the server is running. Then enable DEBUG via env-var of the server, then read stderr.
m-debug.mistakes: Blaming Claude for "not using MCP". In 90% of cases the cause is a faulty tool description or a server auth error.

instructions.title: Custom Instructions
instructions.what: Permanent instructions that Claude considers in every reply — at the account, Project or [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] level.
instructions.why: So you don't repeat "answer in English, concise, no fluff" in every message.
instructions.when: Right when setting up the environment — this is the first investment that pays off from the first conversation.
instructions.impact: Good [[node:instructions|instructions]] = unified tone, style, format across all answers. Without them: each answer feels like a new person — different voice, different structure, no consistency.
instructions.example: I'm a product manager. Reply tersely, in the format "fact, then consequence, then recommendation", without formal preambles.
instructions.mistakes: Writing long rants there like "help me with everything" — the model stops noticing what matters.

i-global.title: Global
i-global.what: Settings in your personal [[node:pl-web-setup|Claude.ai]] profile: apply to all chats unless overridden.
i-global.why: Basic "character": language, tone, format — no need to repeat in every Project.
i-global.when: Once — when setting up the account.
i-global.impact: Without them — every new chat starts from scratch on style.
i-global.example: Always answer in English. Be concise. Use bullet points by default.
i-global.mistakes: Conflicting with [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] — the Project wins, and your global stops working there.

i-project.title: Project level
i-project.what: Inside a Project — overrides/extends globals. A narrowly specialized context.
i-project.why: Makes the Project an "expert" on one topic — without bloating the global.
i-project.when: Every time you create a serious Project.
i-project.impact: Without them the Project = just a folder with files, not a specialized assistant.
i-project.example: You're an expert in my domain. Structure: problem, then impact, then recommendation.
i-project.mistakes: Duplicating global instructions in every Project — extend, don't repeat.

i-claudemd.title: CLAUDE.md (as a file)
i-claudemd.what: Project file in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]: stack, conventions, taboos, critical paths.
i-claudemd.why: These are instructions at the level "how we write code right here".
i-claudemd.when: In every repository that uses [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]].
i-claudemd.impact: Without [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] Claude's code is generic; with it — matches your norms.
i-claudemd.example: Stack: Next.js + Tailwind. Never use any. Tests — Vitest, not Jest.
i-claudemd.mistakes: Describing the obvious there (that it's React) — better to write about non-obvious rules.

i-style.title: Response style
i-style.what: Length, format (bullets / paragraphs), level of formality, use of emoji and humor.
i-style.why: Readability and fit to your habits — otherwise answers are good but "not yours".
i-style.when: When you notice you reword Claude's answers before using them.
i-style.impact: Precise style tuning = answers can be used without edits.
i-style.example: No openers like "great question". No emoji. Headers — H3 max.
i-style.mistakes: Asking to "be friendlier" — too vague; specify the format.

i-templates.title: Templates
i-templates.what: A response template in instructions: format, sections, fields. Claude always delivers in this structure.
i-templates.why: Makes Claude's output integrable — into Notion, tickets, reports.
i-templates.when: When output goes into a standardized system (Jira, report template).
i-templates.impact: A template in instructions = 10× less manual post-processing.
i-templates.example: Report format: ## Problem ## Impact ## Solution ## Effect — always like this.
i-templates.mistakes: Changing the template from chat to chat — you lose the benefit of unification.

prompting.title: Prompt engineering
prompting.what: The discipline of "how to compose a request so the model answers precisely". Structure, context, examples, role.
prompting.why: The same request can be phrased so that quality differs 5-10×.
prompting.when: Every time the task is non-trivial, the answer unsatisfactory, or you need stability.
prompting.impact: This is the cheapest way to raise quality — without changing the model or adding new tools.
prompting.example: You're an expert in my domain. Task: 3 headline options for my material. Audience: <describe briefly>.
prompting.mistakes: A one-liner "do it well" — the most common source of "bad" model answers.

pr-principles.title: Principles
pr-principles.what: Context, then Role, then Task, then Format, then Constraints. The more concrete, the more accurate.
pr-principles.why: It's the base framework that works almost always.
pr-principles.when: Before any non-trivial request, spend 30 seconds on structure.
pr-principles.impact: A structured prompt = an answer you can use without rewriting. Without structure: first draft is "meh", you spend another 15 minutes on clarifications and rewrites.
pr-principles.example: Context: my task. Role: expert in my domain. Task: 5 solution options. Format: table. Constraints: <your own>.
pr-principles.mistakes: Writing the "task" right away without context and role — the model guesses, errs more often.

pr-xml.title: XML tags
pr-xml.what: Claude works excellently with XML markup: <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>.
pr-xml.why: Clear block separation — the model doesn't confuse data with instructions.
pr-xml.when: When the prompt is long or contains several information types.
pr-xml.impact: An XML structure = 2-3× more stable result on complex tasks.
pr-xml.mistakes: Using XML when not needed on simple prompts — it's noise.

pr-fewshot.title: Few-shot examples
pr-fewshot.what: Give 1-3 input-to-output examples — and the model picks up the pattern without explanations.
pr-fewshot.why: This is the strongest technique for non-standard formats and subtle style.
pr-fewshot.when: When the format is hard to describe in words or you need a particular tone.
pr-fewshot.impact: Few-shot = +30-80% format accuracy vs zero-shot explanation.
pr-fewshot.example: Example 1: ... Example 2: ... Now do the same for: ...
pr-fewshot.mistakes: Giving contradictory examples — the model picks a random pattern.

pr-cot.title: Chain of Thought
pr-cot.what: "Think step by step before answering" — the model shows reasoning, then the result.
pr-cot.why: Sharply raises accuracy on logical, mathematical, analytical tasks.
pr-cot.when: When the task isn't "know a fact" but "derive an answer" from conditions.
pr-cot.example: Walk step by step: 1) list the data 2) form hypotheses 3) verify 4) recommend.
pr-cot.mistakes: Using CoT on simple questions — an unnecessarily long answer for nothing.

pr-role.title: Role and context
pr-role.what: "You're an expert in area X with a focus on Y" — sets the level and focus of the answer.
pr-role.why: The model pulls in the relevant "persona" — this changes depth and language.
pr-role.when: When you need an expert level or a specific angle.
pr-role.impact: A good role = +1-2 levels of answer depth.
pr-role.example: You're a security expert. Find vulnerabilities in this code, rank by criticality.
pr-role.mistakes: Vague roles like "you're an expert in everything" — you lose the persona benefit.

pr-prefill.title: Prefill (start the response)
pr-prefill.what: A technique where you set the start of Claude's response in advance — the model continues from that point. In API — the `assistant` field at the start of messages. In chat — the phrase "Start the response like this: ...".
pr-prefill.why: Hard-locks the format and tone from the first character: you don't need to rely on "follow the instruction".
pr-prefill.when: When you need a strict format (JSON, XML, markdown table), a specific heading, refusal of openers, or you want to "jump" straight into the needed reasoning part.
pr-prefill.impact: Prefill gives +50-100% format adherence vs description in words; works where Few-shot overloads the context.
pr-prefill.example: Start the response with exactly `{` — no preamble, only valid JSON per the schema below.
pr-prefill.mistakes: Prefilling a long starting text — the model will "reach" for it, losing quality. 1-3 anchor tokens are enough.

pr-structured.title: Structured output
pr-structured.what: Getting the answer in a strict structure: JSON by schema, XML, markdown table, CSV. Achieved by describing the schema in the prompt + Prefill + an explicit output example.
pr-structured.why: So the output can be parsed automatically and fed into a system: tickets, tables, reports, downstream LLM.
pr-structured.when: When integrating Claude into a pipeline, on batch processing, when after Claude there's a code parser.
pr-structured.impact: Structured output turns a text model into a reliable pipeline component: parses in 99% of cases vs ~70% for free text.
pr-structured.example: Return JSON: {"summary": string (≤200 chars), "risks": [{"id": string, "severity": "low"|"med"|"high"}]}. No preamble, start with {.
pr-structured.mistakes: Asking for "JSON" without a schema and example — Claude will invent fields. Without Prefill — it may add a ```json wrapper or a preamble phrase.

pr-iterate.title: Prompt iteration
pr-iterate.what: A systematic approach to improving a prompt: run, find a concrete failure, make 1 edit (role / example / constraint), repeat. Not "rewrite entirely", but hypothesis, then verification.
pr-iterate.why: Most "bad prompts" turn into "great ones" after 3-5 targeted iterations. Without a method, you either give up or rewrite and lose the working parts.
pr-iterate.when: When the prompt gives ~70% of the result and there's a concrete "I don't like X" — that's exactly the situation where iteration beats rewriting.
pr-iterate.impact: An iterative approach = 5-10× faster than "rewrite from scratch" and preserves working pieces.
pr-iterate.example: Run the prompt on 3 different inputs, then note what's bad in each, then find the common pattern, then add one constraint, then repeat.
pr-iterate.mistakes: Changing 5 things at once — you can't tell what helped. Change one at a time, fix the effect.

ready-prompts.title: Ready-made prompts
ready-prompts.what: A collection of reproducible prompts for typical tasks — examples of ready ones: [[prompt:create-project|"Create a Project"]], [[prompt:create-skill|"Create a Skill"]], [[prompt:create-claudemd|"Create a CLAUDE.md"]], [[prompt:expert-audit|"Expert audit"]].
ready-prompts.why: So you don't "invent the phrasing" every time — there's a working base, tested in practice.
ready-prompts.when: When the task recurs but it's too early to formalize a Skill — you can quickly adapt a prompt.
ready-prompts.impact: Ready-made prompts save 5-15 minutes per task and raise the quality floor.
ready-prompts.example: Open the [[prompt:create-skill|ready-made prompt "Create a Skill"]], plug in your topic — you get a working SKILL.md in a minute.
ready-prompts.mistakes: Using a prompt "as is" without adapting to context — you'll get a generic result.

rp-project.title: Create a Project
rp-project.what: A template for quickly setting up a new Project: role, format, taboos, KPIs.
rp-project.why: All Projects immediately come out professional-grade — not "bare chat".
rp-project.impact: Without a good template a Project = just a folder, not a specialized assistant.
rp-project.mistakes: Copying as is — be sure to plug in your own domain and style.

rp-artifact.title: Create an Artifact
rp-artifact.what: A template for creating a quality HTML/React prototype in a single prompt.
rp-artifact.why: Guarantees preview, responsiveness, baseline accessibility on the first try.
rp-artifact.when: When you need an interactive prototype, not a text description.
rp-artifact.impact: A good prompt = 1-2 iterations instead of 5-7.
rp-artifact.example: Open the [[prompt:html-prototype|ready-made prompt "Create an HTML prototype"]].
rp-artifact.mistakes: Not specifying target audience and device — you'll get generic markup.

rp-skill.title: Create a Skill
rp-skill.what: Prompt template for skill-creator: role, steps, templates, triggers.
rp-skill.why: Turns an idea into a working Skill in one pass.
rp-skill.when: When you have an established practice and want to formalize it.
rp-skill.impact: Without a template the Skill often "doesn't trigger" because of a bad trigger.
rp-skill.mistakes: Not specifying triggers explicitly — the Skill won't activate when needed.

rp-claudemd.title: Create CLAUDE.md
rp-claudemd.what: A prompt to generate [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] with the right structure: stack, conventions, taboos, entry points.
rp-claudemd.why: A ready project file in 1 minute — not an hour of manual formatting.
rp-claudemd.when: In every project where you run [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]].
rp-claudemd.impact: [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] from a template = the model writes code "in project style" right away.
rp-claudemd.mistakes: Not specifying taboos — Claude will use patterns forbidden in the project.

rp-audit.title: Expert audit
rp-audit.what: A prompt checklist: structure, clarity, risks, principle alignment, final recommendation.
rp-audit.why: Covers 80% of typical issues in one pass.
rp-audit.when: Before launching something new or after a major change.
rp-audit.impact: A structured audit = actions instead of opinions.
rp-audit.example: Open the [[prompt:expert-audit|ready-made prompt "Run an expert audit"]].
rp-audit.mistakes: Not specifying context and audience — recommendations will be detached from reality.

scenarios.title: Use cases
scenarios.what: Typical tasks where Claude delivers max value: code, design, content, research, analysis.
scenarios.why: So you see where to apply the tool right away — without long "where will it help me?".
scenarios.when: At the start of Claude work — define 1-2 of your scenarios and deepen them.
scenarios.impact: Understanding the scenario, then choosing the right tool (Project / Skill / Code / Artifact).
scenarios.example: I have a regular task — <describe>. What scenario and tool stack is optimal?
scenarios.mistakes: Using Claude everywhere "a little bit" — nowhere will you get to expert level.

sc-analysis.title: Analysis and audit
sc-analysis.what: Expert audit, code review, document audit, security review.
sc-analysis.why: Claude is strongest where deep analysis and weighed conclusions are needed.
sc-analysis.when: When you have an artifact (page, code, document) and need conclusions.
sc-analysis.impact: A good prompt + Project = an audit at a competent expert's level in minutes.
sc-analysis.example: Run an audit of this material against a clear set of criteria (structure, clarity, risks).
sc-analysis.mistakes: Asking "give an evaluation" without criteria — you'll get generic phrases.

sc-coding.title: Programming
sc-coding.what: Code writing, refactoring, debugging, migrations, tests — especially in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]].
sc-coding.why: Claude is one of the best coding models; combined with the CLI it becomes almost an intern.
sc-coding.when: Any development from prototype to production.
sc-coding.impact: Works stronger with [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] and Hooks — otherwise it drifts into its own habits.
sc-coding.example: Rewrite this endpoint so it uses transactions and caches the result for 60s.
sc-coding.mistakes: Working in chat, not in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — you lose file and history access.

sc-design.title: Design and UX
sc-design.what: Prototypes, UX copy, design critique, accessibility audit — especially with Figma MCP.
sc-design.why: Claude sees the design, understands context, suggests options — at the level of a competent expert.
sc-design.when: Any task from research to handoff — there are ready-made Skills (design:*).
sc-design.impact: When Claude sees the system itself via MCP — work quality with it rises especially sharply.
sc-design.example: Open this layout, do a design critique and propose 3 improvements to the hero section.
sc-design.mistakes: Doing design "through text" without screenshots and real mockups — you lose half the context.

sc-content.title: Content
sc-content.what: Long-reads, social posts, email, documentation, translations.
sc-content.why: Claude is good at sensing tone, brand voice — especially with examples.
sc-content.when: When you need text you wouldn't be embarrassed to publish.
sc-content.impact: With a Project and a brand guide — you get texts "in voice" without editing.
sc-content.example: Write a 1500-word longread about IT burnout — in our tone (examples above).
sc-content.mistakes: Asking to "write a post" without audience and tone — you'll get generic output.

sc-research.title: Research
sc-research.what: Analysis of articles, competitors, market, synthesis of interviews, literature reviews.
sc-research.why: Claude is good at synthesis — extract patterns from 50 sources in minutes.
sc-research.when: When you need to "read everything, find the essential, formulate conclusions".
sc-research.impact: With design:research-synthesis — you get a report at the level of a UX researcher.
sc-research.example: Here are 12 interview transcripts — find 5 key themes and prioritize the problems.
sc-research.mistakes: Asking for a "market overview" without criteria and format — you'll get fluff.

sc-data.title: Data analysis
sc-data.what: CSV / XLSX / JSON / SQL dumps — Claude reads, computes aggregates, looks for anomalies, plots charts. Especially strong with [[node:cap-code-exec|Code execution]]: real numbers, not approximations.
sc-data.why: To move from Excel formulas to human language: "find top-5 SKUs with revenue drops and explain the pattern" — without VLOOKUP.
sc-data.when: When there's a data table and questions like "what's interesting here", "what's anomalous", "what are the trends".
sc-data.impact: Removes the "tool tax": instead of an hour on formulas — minutes of conversation with the data.
sc-data.example: Upload a CSV of orders, then "Find SKUs with a >30% drop in March vs February. Show top-5 with possible causes from available columns".
sc-data.mistakes: Asking to "analyze the data" without a question — you'll get a generic description. Good analysis starts from a concrete question.

b-educators.title: Claude for educators
b-educators.what: Claude handles the preparation routine: lesson plans, explanations at different levels, assignments, quizzes, feedback — freeing time for real interaction with students.
b-educators.why: Educators spend up to 40% of their working time preparing materials. Claude cuts that time 3–5× without sacrificing quality.
b-educators.when: When planning a lesson, developing differentiated tasks, writing personalised feedback, or explaining complex concepts at multiple levels.
b-educators.impact: 5–10 hours saved per week; more differentiated materials; the teacher focuses on pedagogical judgment rather than routine text.
b-educators.example: "Explain photosynthesis in three ways: for a 6-year-old, a 12-year-old, and a biology undergraduate" — three ready explanations in seconds.
b-educators.mistakes: Letting Claude evaluate all student work without review — the teacher's pedagogical judgment is irreplaceable; Claude only speeds up the draft feedback.

agents.title: Agent ideas
agents.what: Ready-made Subagent templates for routines: reviewer, auditor, researcher, technical writer, manager assistant.
agents.why: To turn a repeating process into a button — without manual prompting every time.
agents.when: When you catch yourself thinking "I'm explaining the same thing again".
agents.impact: A good agent = -80% time on a typical task.
agents.example: Create a Subagent for your regular task: description, role, report template, and trigger by keywords.
agents.mistakes: Building an agent for a task that occurs once a month — no payoff.

ag-principles.title: Agent design principles
ag-principles.what: A good agent: narrow purpose, clear trigger, limited tool set, explicit fallback paths, observability (logs / metrics), idempotency for dangerous actions. Without these 6 properties an agent is just a long prompt.
ag-principles.why: Most "non-working" agents fail on one of these. Principles are a checklist before launch, not "best practices" after the fact.
ag-principles.when: Before creating any agent — walk through the principles as a filter. If on 2+ points you "didn't think about it" — the agent isn't ready.
ag-principles.impact: Design by principles = 3-5× fewer "weird behaviors" in prod; easier to debug, easier to hand off to the team.
ag-principles.example: Trigger: "review PR". Tools: only git diff + Read. Fallback: if diff > 1000 lines — ask the user to narrow scope. Observability: log to .claude/logs/code-reviewer.jsonl.
ag-principles.mistakes: Giving the agent 30 tools "just in case" — it'll pick the wrong ones. A narrow surface = more reliable.

ag-code.title: Code Reviewer
ag-code.what: An agent that checks PRs/commits against a checklist: security, readability, tests, regressions.
ag-code.why: Lifts the pre-review routine off a human — they see the already filtered stuff.
ag-code.when: In every repository with a PR process.
ag-code.impact: Review quality grows, expert time saves multifold.
ag-code.example: Subagent code-reviewer: trigger "review PR", output — list of comments by severity.
ag-code.mistakes: Trusting only the agent — doesn't replace the expert's architectural thinking.

ag-ux.title: Audit Agent
ag-ux.what: An agent takes input material and produces an audit by fixed criteria.
ag-ux.why: Needed everywhere there are regular releases and a pre-release check.
ag-ux.when: When there's no time for a manual full audit but you need a signal "is it okay?".
ag-ux.impact: Ideal paired with an MCP server to the relevant system and topical Skills.
ag-ux.example: Agent auditor: input — material, output — top-N problems sorted by impact.
ag-ux.mistakes: Replacing checks with real users by this — the agent has hypotheses, people have facts.

ag-research.title: Researcher
ag-research.what: An agent searches sources, synthesizes, delivers a report with references — for marketing or product.
ag-research.why: Removes 70% of the "dirty" work: reading, note-taking, citing.
ag-research.when: Before a product launch, in competitor analysis, market overview.
ag-research.impact: With [[node:cap-search|Web search]] + a topical Skill — delivers quality of a competent analyst.
ag-research.example: Agent researcher: topic + 3 questions, then 2-page report with sources and a comparison table.
ag-research.mistakes: Accepting conclusions without verifying sources — the model can hallucinate links.

ag-designer.title: Designer Assistant
ag-designer.what: An on-demand agent: design critique, UX copy, component variants, accessibility check.
ag-designer.why: A discussion partner — asks questions, suggests alternatives, catches flaws.
ag-designer.when: In a design team during research and iteration — before handoff.
ag-designer.impact: Replaces the "second pair of eyes" when a colleague is busy, plus faster.
ag-designer.example: Agent designer-buddy: input is layout / URL, then 5 observations + 3 alternative ideas.
ag-designer.mistakes: Expecting flawless artistic taste from it — it's strong in heuristics, not aesthetics.

ag-pm.title: PM Assistant
ag-pm.what: An agent writes user stories, formulates acceptance criteria, breaks down tasks, prepares standup updates.
ag-pm.why: Frees the PM from formulation routine — leaves time for strategy.
ag-pm.when: In product teams with an active backlog and sprints.
ag-pm.impact: Less misalignment with the team — tasks are clear and uniform.
ag-pm.example: Agent pm-assistant: task statement, then User story + AC + risks + size estimate.
ag-pm.mistakes: Replacing stakeholder interviews with generation — hypotheses ≠ user needs.

cap-thinking.title: Extended thinking (when to enable)
cap-thinking.what:
Extended thinking is a mode where Claude reasons **step-by-step in a hidden thinking block** before answering. The model explores approaches, checks itself, discards bad hypotheses — only then produces the final response.

Available on Claude Opus and Sonnet via the API parameter `thinking: { type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N }`. In claude.ai it's activated via the "Extended thinking" toggle in the input bar.
cap-thinking.why:
Important — this is **not "magically makes Claude smarter"**. It's a tool for a specific class of tasks: those requiring explicitly sequential multi-step reasoning where an error in one step cascades and breaks the result.

For a product/ops team: thinking mode pays off when the cost of an error is higher than the cost of 5× the time and 2-3× the tokens.
cap-thinking.when:
**Enable thinking when:**
- Multi-step reasoning: a chain of 3+ dependent decisions (architecture design, debugging a complex bug)
- Math/logic: tasks where constants and conditions must be held in memory
- Ambiguous prompts: when interpretations must be checked explicitly before action
- Code review: analyzing architectural trade-offs
- High-stakes decisions: rare-but-critical actions (DB migration, deployment plan)

**Do NOT enable thinking when:**
- Simple questions (summarize, translate, format)
- Streaming UX where low latency matters
- Tool use where Claude needs to quickly decide which tool to call
- Bulk operations (1000s of similar tasks — burns money without gain)
cap-thinking.impact:
**Trade-offs:**
- Time: 3-5× slower than a regular response (thinking itself takes 5-30 seconds)
- Cost: 2-3× more expensive in tokens (thinking blocks are billed too)
- Accuracy: significantly higher on complex tasks (per Anthropic benchmarks — up to 30-50% on math/code)

**Real signal:** if you're picking Opus over Sonnet for a complex task — try Sonnet + thinking first. Often equal accuracy at half the cost.
cap-thinking.example:
**Good case** — debugging:
```
thinking: enabled, budget: 8000
prompt: "Production fails with 502 every 2 hours. Logs attached.
         Find root cause."
```
Claude in the thinking block: checks hypotheses (memory leak, race condition, external dep), discards those incompatible with logs, produces final answer with reasoning.

**Bad case** — summarize:
```
thinking: enabled
prompt: "Summarize this email in 3 bullets."
```
Thinking doesn't help here, just burns tokens. Should be thinking: disabled.
cap-thinking.mistakes:
**1. "I enable thinking everywhere by default"** — the most expensive anti-pattern. On simple tasks it adds +200-300% cost without accuracy gain. Use the decision criteria above.

**2. "I never enable thinking"** — you lose accuracy in decision-critical scenarios. If debugging takes 30 min manually, then thinking in 15 seconds saves time × money.

**3. Ignoring budget_tokens** — default budget may be too low/high. A math task with budget=1000 — Claude doesn't reach the answer. A simple task with budget=20000 — burn money. Tune per use case.

**4. Using thinking output for UX** — the thinking block is designed for INTERNAL reasoning, not for the user. Don't show it in production UI without editing.

ag-managed.title: Claude Managed Agents
ag-managed.what: Official Anthropic product: a ready-made, configurable agent harness that runs in managed cloud infrastructure. Handles long-running tasks asynchronously — you submit a task, the agent runs, you poll for results.
ag-managed.why: Building a reliable agent loop from scratch (retries, timeouts, state, observability) takes weeks. Managed Agents provides this out of the box.
ag-managed.when: Long-running tasks (minutes to hours), asynchronous work, production agent deployments that need reliability and scalability.
ag-managed.impact: Cuts agent infrastructure work from weeks to hours. Production-grade reliability without custom DevOps.
ag-managed.example: Submit a task: "research this topic and write a report". Managed Agent runs, uses [[node:cap-search|web search]] and file tools, returns structured results when done.
ag-managed.mistakes: Using Managed Agents for simple single-turn tasks — overkill. Use the Messages API directly for those.

cc-grp-session.title: Session management
cc-grp-session.what:
Session commands in Claude Code — managing context, switching devices, restoring state.

**Context control:**
- [[node:cc-cmd-clear|/clear]] — new session from scratch
- [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]] — compress history, keep conclusions
- /resume — continue previous session
- /rewind — roll back code and chat to a previous state

**Conversation control:**
- /rename — name the conversation
- /branch — fork the conversation at current point
- /recap — short session summary
- /export — save conversation to file
- /copy — copy last response

**Switching devices:**
- /background — keep working after closing terminal
- /desktop — move to [[node:pl-desktop|Claude Desktop]]
- /teleport — continue from [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]
- /remote-control — control from phone

**Exit:**
- /exit — close the CLI
cc-grp-session.why: Sessions are persistent — you can pause, resume, fork, and export any conversation. Understanding session commands prevents losing context.
cc-grp-session.when: Long coding sessions, switching devices, saving progress, recovering from mistakes with /rewind.
cc-grp-session.impact: Never lose work. Resume complex multi-hour tasks. Fork experiments without breaking the main session.
cc-grp-session.example: /branch before a risky refactor, then experiment freely, and if it fails, original session intact.
cc-grp-session.mistakes: Using [[node:cc-cmd-clear|/clear]] when you meant [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]] — /clear deletes context, /compact summarizes it.

cc-grp-context.title: Context and code
cc-grp-context.what: /add-dir — add a directory to Claude's working context. /context — visualize current context usage as a grid. /memory — edit [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] memory files. /diff — view uncommitted changes and per-turn diffs. /focus — show only prompt, tool summary, and final response. /goal — set a goal and keep working until condition met. [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] — generate CLAUDE.md for current project.
cc-grp-context.why: Claude's [[node:b-context|context window]] is finite. These commands let you control what Claude sees and focus its attention.
cc-grp-context.when: Large codebases (add only relevant dirs), long sessions (monitor with /context), starting new projects ([[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]]).
cc-grp-context.impact: Better answers, fewer hallucinations, faster responses — Claude sees exactly what it needs.
cc-grp-context.example: /add-dir src/components, then Claude now reads all component files without you referencing each one.
cc-grp-context.mistakes: Adding the entire repo when only one folder is relevant — wastes context and slows Claude down.

cc-grp-model.title: Model and limits
cc-grp-model.what: /model — switch the AI model for current session. /fast — toggle fast mode (uses Haiku). /effort — set effort level for model usage. /advisor — consult a stronger model at key moments. /upgrade — upgrade to Max for higher limits. /usage — show session cost, plan usage, activity stats. /status — show [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] version, model, account, API connectivity. /extra-usage — configure extra usage when limits hit.
cc-grp-model.why: Different tasks need different models. Switching mid-session saves cost without losing context.
cc-grp-model.when: Use /fast for quick edits, /model for architecture work, /usage to track spend, /status to diagnose connection issues.
cc-grp-model.impact: Significant cost savings. Correct model for each task. Never hit limits unexpectedly.
cc-grp-model.example: /fast for writing tests, then /model Opus for the tricky algorithm, then back to /fast for cleanup.
cc-grp-model.mistakes: Never checking /usage — unexpected bill at end of month.

cc-grp-ui.title: Interface and appearance
cc-grp-ui.what: /color — set prompt bar color for this session. /theme — change the overall theme. /tui — set terminal UI renderer (default or fullscreen). /terminal-setup — enable Option+Enter for newlines and visual bell. /voice — toggle voice mode. /focus — show minimal output (prompt + summary + response only). /radio — Claude FM lo-fi background music. /stickers — order physical [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] stickers.
cc-grp-ui.why: A comfortable interface reduces friction during long coding sessions.
cc-grp-ui.when: /theme and /color for visual clarity. /terminal-setup once after install. /focus when output is too noisy.
cc-grp-ui.impact: Less cognitive load. Better readability in long sessions.
cc-grp-ui.example: /theme dark + /color #d97757, then visually distinct Claude terminal from other windows.
cc-grp-ui.mistakes: Skipping /terminal-setup — Option+Enter won't work for multi-line prompts on macOS.

cc-grp-config.title: Configuration and settings
cc-grp-config.what: /config — open the config panel. /keybindings — open or create keybindings config file. /permissions — manage allow and deny tool permission rules. /privacy-settings — view and update privacy settings. /update-config — configure settings.json via natural language. /sandbox — configure sandbox for tool execution. /remote-env — configure default remote environment.
cc-grp-config.why: Permissions and keybindings are core to safe, efficient [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] usage. Misconfigured permissions = constant approval prompts.
cc-grp-config.when: /permissions after first install to allowlist common tools. /keybindings to set Cmd+Enter as submit. /config for one-stop settings overview.
cc-grp-config.impact: Fewer interruptions, faster workflow, safer execution.
cc-grp-config.example: /permissions, then allow 'Bash(npm run *)', then Claude can run npm scripts without asking every time.
cc-grp-config.mistakes: Allowing all bash commands globally — security risk. Be specific: 'Bash(npm run *)' not 'Bash(*)'.

cc-grp-integrations.title: Integrations
cc-grp-integrations.what: /mcp — manage MCP servers (add, remove, list). /ide — manage IDE integrations (VS Code, JetBrains) and show status. /chrome — Claude in Chrome beta settings. /hooks — view hook configurations for tool events. /plugin — manage [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] plugins. /reload-plugins — activate pending plugin changes. /agents — manage agent configurations. /install-github-app — set up Claude GitHub Actions. /install-slack-app — install Claude Slack app. /web-setup — setup Claude Code on the web.
cc-grp-integrations.why: Integrations extend [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] into your full development workflow — IDE, GitHub, Slack, browser.
cc-grp-integrations.when: /ide after installing VS Code extension. /mcp to connect databases or APIs. /hooks for pre/post-tool automation.
cc-grp-integrations.impact: Claude works inside your existing tools instead of alongside them.
cc-grp-integrations.example: /ide, then VS Code integration active, then Claude sees open files and inline diagnostics automatically.
cc-grp-integrations.mistakes: /reload-plugins not called after adding a plugin — new plugin won't activate until next session.

cc-grp-automation.title: Automation and AI tasks
cc-grp-automation.what: /plan — enable [[node:cc-plan-mode|plan mode]] or view current session plan. /autofix-pr — monitor and autofix issues with current PR. /tasks — list and manage background tasks. /loop — run a prompt or command on recurring interval. /schedule — create scheduled remote agent routines. /batch — plan a large-scale change, execute across 5-30 parallel worktree agents. /ultraplan — draft a plan on the web for editing and approval. /ultrareview — deep bug finding ($5-20, runs on web). /goal — set a completion condition and keep working until met. /background — continue session in background.
cc-grp-automation.why: These commands turn Claude from a chat assistant into an autonomous worker that runs tasks while you focus elsewhere.
cc-grp-automation.when: /loop for recurring tasks. /batch for large refactors across many files. /schedule for nightly automation. /ultrareview before major releases.
cc-grp-automation.impact: Hours of work compressed into background tasks. Claude handles parallelism you couldn't manage manually.
cc-grp-automation.example: /batch 'add JSDoc to all functions in src/', then 20 parallel agents, each opens a PR for their file group.
cc-grp-automation.mistakes: Running /batch without /plan first — always approve the plan before parallel execution.

cc-grp-quality.title: Code quality and review
cc-grp-quality.what: /review — review a pull request with structured analysis. /security-review — security review of pending branch changes. /simplify — review changed code for reuse, quality, efficiency. /debug — enable debug logging for session diagnostics. /fewer-permission-prompts — scan transcripts, build allowlist to reduce permission interruptions. /diff — view uncommitted changes and per-turn diffs.
cc-grp-quality.why: These are the quality gates before shipping. Claude catches what linters miss: logic errors, security issues, over-engineering.
cc-grp-quality.when: Before every PR merge: /review. Before deploy: /security-review. After a long session: /simplify.
cc-grp-quality.impact: Fewer bugs in production. Cleaner code. Security issues caught before they ship.
cc-grp-quality.example: /review, then Claude lists issues by severity: Critical (SQL injection risk), Warning (no error handling), Info (rename for clarity).
cc-grp-quality.mistakes: Using /review as a rubber stamp — read the output carefully, especially Critical items.

cc-grp-help.title: Help, learning and account
cc-grp-help.what: /help — show all available commands. /powerup — discover [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] features through quick interactive lessons. /release-notes — view what's new. /btw — ask a side question without interrupting main task. /insights — analyze your Claude Code session patterns. /skills — list available installed skills. /team-onboarding — generate a guide for teammates. /login / /logout — account management. /feedback — submit feedback to Anthropic. /doctor — diagnose installation issues. /mobile — QR code for mobile app.
cc-grp-help.why: Onboarding and ongoing learning. /btw and /insights are underused gems.
cc-grp-help.when: /doctor when something breaks. /powerup when starting out. /btw for quick questions mid-task. /insights weekly to see your usage patterns.
cc-grp-help.impact: /btw alone saves dozens of context-breaking interruptions per day.
cc-grp-help.example: Mid-refactor: /btw what does the Builder pattern solve? Then Claude answers briefly, then main task continues.
cc-grp-help.mistakes: Never running /doctor when CLI behaves strangely — it catches 90% of common issues instantly.

pl-cowork.title: Claude Cowork
pl-cowork.what: Agentic task automation built into [[node:pl-desktop|Claude Desktop]] (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise). Claude plans multi-step work, breaks it into subtasks, runs code in an isolated VM on your machine, and writes results directly to your file system. Unlike chat, you describe an outcome — Claude handles every step.
pl-cowork.why: Complex knowledge work — file organization, data analysis, document creation — requires many coordinated steps and local file access. Cowork handles this autonomously so you can step away and come back to finished results.
pl-cowork.when: Organizing a chaotic folder, processing hundreds of receipts, synthesizing research from multiple documents, building spreadsheets with formulas, creating reports. NOT for simple questions — use regular chat instead.
pl-cowork.impact: Hours of repetitive file and document work done while you focus on other things. Can run scheduled tasks automatically (daily, weekly) without any code or APIs.
pl-cowork.example: Task: Sort my Downloads folder by type, extract total amounts from all receipt screenshots, create an Excel report with monthly totals. Claude plans the steps, reads files, runs analysis, and saves the finished spreadsheet — all without your involvement.
pl-cowork.mistakes: Using Cowork for simple Q&A — wastes your usage quota significantly. Closing the Desktop app while a task runs — this stops it immediately. Granting access to your entire drive — connect only the folder you need.

pl-integrations.title: Integrations
pl-integrations.what: Claude connects to external apps and platforms via built-in connectors. Key integrations: Chrome extension (reads/navigates/fills forms in your browser, side panel, tab groups, scheduled browser tasks — paid plans, beta). Microsoft 365 (read-only access to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Word, Excel, PowerPoint — all plans). Google Workspace (Drive, Gmail, Calendar via Plus menu connectors). Slack (search messages, meeting transcripts).
pl-integrations.why: Keeps Claude inside your existing workflow instead of requiring you to copy-paste content between apps. Claude sees the context you're already working in.
pl-integrations.when: Chrome: automating repetitive browser tasks, extracting data from websites, filling forms. M365: asking questions about your emails, documents, meetings without leaving Claude. Google: referencing Drive files or calendar events in chat. Slack: finding past decisions or meeting summaries.
pl-integrations.impact: Eliminates the biggest friction in AI workflows — manually moving context between tools. Claude becomes a layer on top of your existing apps.
pl-integrations.example: Enable M365 connector, then ask Claude: 'Summarize the emails from last week about the budget proposal and list open action items.' Claude searches Outlook and Teams, reads the threads, and returns a structured summary.
pl-integrations.mistakes: Expecting M365/Google connectors to take actions (send emails, create docs) — they are READ-ONLY for now. Not granting the necessary permissions when installing Chrome extension — Claude can't see page content without them.

cap-limitations.title: Capabilities & Limitations
cap-limitations.what:
Claude is powerful, but has real limits. Knowing them = not being surprised or frustrated when something doesn't work.

**Key limits:**
- **Knowledge cutoff** — training data ends around early 2026. Claude doesn't know events after that.
- **Hallucinations** — may confidently state false facts, especially on niche topics or while "filling gaps".
- **No real-time data** — without web search enabled, can't see the internet.
- **[[node:b-context|Context window]]** — in long conversations early content "falls out" of memory.
- **No image generation** — text and code only (use Imagen / DALL-E / etc. for drawing).
- **Literal interpretation** — weak at catching sarcasm, cultural nuance, subtext.
cap-limitations.why: Most AI mistakes happen because users don't know the boundaries. Understanding limitations lets you design prompts and workflows that work around them instead of running into them.
cap-limitations.when: Any time you use Claude for factual claims, recent events, long-running tasks, or high-stakes decisions — verify outputs. Never rely solely on Claude for legal, medical, or financial advice.
cap-limitations.impact: Users who understand limitations make 3-5x fewer errors. They verify outputs, use [[node:cap-search|web search]] when needed, break long tasks into shorter sessions, and treat Claude as a first draft rather than a final source.
cap-limitations.example: Bad: 'What is the current stock price of Apple?' — Claude will either refuse or hallucinate. Good: Enable [[node:cap-search|web search]], or ask Claude to reason from what it knows and flag what needs verification.
cap-limitations.mistakes: Treating Claude's confident tone as a signal of accuracy — it is not. Assuming Claude knows recent events — its training has a cutoff. Using one long chat for a multi-day project — context degrades. Not verifying facts on critical documents.

pr-4d.title: 4D Framework
pr-4d.what: Anthropic's meta-framework for effective AI collaboration, co-developed with Ringling College and University College Cork. Four skills that apply to every AI interaction regardless of model or tool: Delegation (choosing what to give AI), Description (writing clear prompts), Discernment (evaluating output critically), Diligence (iterating until the result is safe and accurate). Defines 24 specific behaviors of effective AI use.
pr-4d.why: Most AI failures happen at one of these four stages, not because of the model. A strong prompt to the wrong task (bad Delegation), a correct task with a vague prompt (bad Description), accepting hallucinated output (bad Discernment), or publishing an unverified first draft (bad Diligence). Fixing the stage fixes the failure.
pr-4d.when: Use as a checklist before every significant AI task: Am I delegating the right work? Is my prompt specific enough? Did I verify the output? Is this iteration ready to use? Takes 30 seconds — saves hours of rework.
pr-4d.impact: Users who internalize the 4D Framework produce reliable AI output consistently. It is transferable across all AI tools — skills do not become obsolete when models change.
pr-4d.example: Delegation: 'This research synthesis is suitable for AI.' Description: 'Summarize these 5 articles into 3 key themes for a non-technical audience, max 200 words each.' Discernment: 'Claude cited a statistic I cannot verify — flag it.' Diligence: 'Revise theme 2 — it misses the regulatory angle from article 3.'
pr-4d.mistakes: Skipping Delegation — giving AI tasks that require human judgment (ethical decisions, relationship-sensitive communications). Skipping Discernment — publishing AI output without fact-checking. Stopping at one iteration — Diligence means feedback loops, not a single send.

foundation.title: Claude Foundation
foundation.what:
The base layer: what Claude actually is, how it works, what its limits are. Everything else — [[node:systems|Systems]], [[node:transformation|Transformation]], [[node:use-cases|Use Cases]] — relies on this.

When you read about RAG, multi-agent or workflows in other sections — you'll come back here for context: what model, what [[node:b-context|context window]], what costs.
foundation.why:
Without the Foundation layer the rest is magic. You won't understand why something works one day and not the next, why one model is 15× cheaper than another, why your prompt does fine in chat and breaks in production.

This is the layer where "AI feels like magic" turns into "I know what's going on under the hood".
foundation.when:
Start here if you're new to Claude. Come back here when something stops working in the other layers and you don't understand why.

If you've worked with Claude for 6+ months — you probably know 70% of this. Skim, look for blind spots.
foundation.impact:
After Foundation: you stop being surprised. You know which model to pick for which task. You don't burn through budget on "just to be safe". You don't blame the model when in fact your prompt is the problem.

Main effect: you understand the tool instead of believing in it.
foundation.example:
A typical Foundation question: "Why does Claude give a great answer in chat but trip in the API?"

Answer in Foundation language: in chat you have system prompts from Anthropic + Projects context + conversation history. In the API — you have only what you sent. Same model, different context. Once you get it — you stop being surprised by 80% of "weird" cases.
foundation.mistakes:
Main mistake: skip the basics and dive into "cool stuff" like multi-agent. Six months in you'll be debugging things you don't understand because you skipped the foundation.

Better: spend 2-3 hours on Foundation, then move on. Faster overall than "learn as you go".

systems.title: Systems — how AI works as a system
systems.what:
[[node:foundation|Foundation]] is about "Claude can do X". Systems is about "how to make Claude do X every day, predictably, in a team".

This is the layer where you move from "playing in chat" to "we have a working process". Workflows, data, integrations, monitoring — the things that turn AI from a toy into a tool.
systems.why:
AI in chat is fun, but it doesn't scale. Five people, five different ways to do the same thing. No idea what the team did yesterday. Costs unclear, quality drifting, model changed — what now?

Systems is the answer to all of this. Not "how to write a better prompt", but "how to build something stable".
systems.when:
When you notice:
- AI helps you, but the team uses it however they want — chaos
- You've automated something — now you have no idea if it's still working
- AI costs are growing, no one knows why
- You want to scale your AI experiment from "on the manager's laptop" to "the whole team uses this"
systems.impact:
Without Systems: 80% of AI initiatives die at the pilot stage. "It worked, then quality dropped, no one fixed it."

With Systems: AI features live for years. You see problems in a day, not a month. The team trusts the process — they don't need to check every output manually.

Main point: AI stops being magic and becomes infrastructure.
systems.example:
A typical Systems question: "AI writes email drafts well, but how do we make sure nothing weird ever goes to a client?"

The answer involves several Systems building blocks at once: workflow with steps, quality gate before sending, escalation to a human on edge cases, eval to monitor quality weekly, cost management not to overspend.

That's the difference between "AI helps a manager" and "the team has reliable support powered by AI".
systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: jump into Systems without Foundation. You'll be building workflows without understanding how the model works underneath. You'll be confused why one chain works and another doesn't.

Second mistake: build a System for an unimportant task. Systems take effort. Build them where it matters — frequent, business-critical work. Don't automate something you do once a month.

transformation.title: Transformation — how AI changes the way a team works
transformation.what:
[[node:foundation|Foundation]] = "what Claude can do". [[node:systems|Systems]] = "how to make Claude work like a system". Transformation = "how a team's work changes when AI becomes a real part of it".

This is about changes in your role. Marketer turns from a copywriter into a brand strategist. Designer — from a pixel-pusher into a researcher. Support — from "answering tickets" into "improving the product".
transformation.why:
Tools alone don't change the company. You can buy ChatGPT for everyone and nothing happens — people will keep working the old way.

Real transformation = a change in how teams work, what they measure, what they consider their job. That's the hardest and most valuable part.
transformation.when:
When you sense:
- We have AI tools — but the way we work hasn't really changed
- Each team uses AI on its own — no shared practice
- AI changed individuals — but the team is still organized the same
- Hard to articulate "so what specifically changed in our role"
transformation.impact:
Without Transformation: AI = an individual tool. Everyone uses it differently, no team-wide impact, the leadership can't show what changed.

With Transformation: the team's role visibly shifts in a year. You don't talk about "AI" anymore — you talk about "how we work now". AI is a given, not a feature.

Main point: AI stops being a topic for separate meetings and becomes the new default of how the team works.
transformation.example:
Marketing team before transformation: 3 posts a week, content plans always slipping, brand voice fuzzy, analytics "someday".

A year into transformation: 15 posts a week, brand voice configured in AI (everyone writes consistently), daily analytics in Slack, the team focuses on strategy and creative directions, not on "who's writing what".

The difference isn't "AI tools" — it's a different team that works differently.
transformation.mistakes:
Main mistake: skip Foundation and Systems, jump straight to Transformation. "We're transforming, AI everywhere!" — without solid building blocks underneath the transformation is fake.

Second mistake: top-down transformation. "Everyone now works with AI" in a CEO email = two weeks later everyone is back to the old ways. You need bottom-up traction from teams + top-down support.

Third mistake: measuring transformation in productivity %. Real transformation = a change in what the team considers important and how it spends its time. That's hard to put into a single %.

use-cases.title: Use Cases — ready-made scenarios for your task
use-cases.what:
[[node:foundation|Foundation]] / [[node:systems|Systems]] / [[node:transformation|Transformation]] answer "what / how / why". Use Cases answer "here's exactly what to do for this specific task".

A Use Case is a path: "I need to organize support — read these 5 nodes in this order, watch these 2 tutorials, you'll get a working system in 2 weeks".

It's a shortcut from "there's tons of stuff in the knowledge base" to "here's the path for your situation".
use-cases.why:
The knowledge base has hundreds of nodes. Most people can't and won't read all of it. They want "I need X — show me what to read for that".

Use Cases are pre-assembled answers to the most common "I need X". You don't think about which nodes are relevant — you follow the path.
use-cases.when:
Start with a Use Case when:
- You have a specific business task (organize support, set up brand voice, automate operations)
- You don't know where to start in the knowledge base
- You want to see how nodes connect into a real solution
- You need a result in 2-4 weeks, not "learn AI in general"
use-cases.impact:
Without Use Cases: you spend 2 weeks reading the knowledge base, get tons of theory but no clear answer to "what do I actually do".

With Use Cases: 2 hours through the path, then a clear plan, then 2 weeks of implementation, then measurable result.

Main point: knowledge leads to action, not knowledge leading to more knowledge.
use-cases.example:
Use Case "AI in support": you read 5 specific nodes (tier-1 automation, knowledge base, escalation, evals, cost management) + watch 2 tutorials about prompt and Project setup, then in 2 weeks you have an AI handling 60% of typical tickets.

If you tried to do this from scratch through the knowledge base — you'd spend a month reading first.
use-cases.mistakes:
Main mistake: think a Use Case will solve everything for you. No — it shows the path. You still have to walk it: read, configure, test on your data.

Second mistake: try to apply someone else's Use Case verbatim to your company. Use Cases are templates. Take 80% from the template, adapt 20% to your specifics.

ai-fundamentals.title: AI Fundamentals
ai-fundamentals.what: Universal AI concepts not tied to any single model: LLM, [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]], vector databases, RAG. The vocabulary every AI system speaks — from ChatGPT to your own pipeline on open-source models.
ai-fundamentals.why: 105 Atlas covers Claude in depth, but the AI industry is broader. To talk with engineers, evaluate vendor proposals, and make architectural decisions — you need the common concepts.
ai-fundamentals.when: When reading a technical doc / proposal with AI terms. When choosing a tech stack. When discussing architecture with your team.
ai-fundamentals.impact: Knowing fundamentals shifts you from "I use AI" to "I understand what I am doing". You gain confidence in decisions and substantive arguments.
ai-fundamentals.example: A RAG pipeline uses [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] (a fundamental concept), stores them in a [[node:af-vector-db|vector database]] (a fundamental technology), and feeds relevant chunks into an LLM (a fundamental architecture). Knowing all three — you can read any RAG documentation.
ai-fundamentals.mistakes: Learning fundamentals as abstract theory. More effective: take a concrete task (e.g., "build search over my docs") and learn the needed concepts as you go.

af-llm-basics.title: What an LLM actually is — plain language
af-llm-basics.what:
You know how iPhone suggests the next word as you type a text? "I'll be..." and the phone offers "home / late / there soon". An LLM does the same — predicts the next word based on what came before. Only it wasn't trained on your texts, but on a huge slice of the internet: Wikipedia, books, articles, forums.

Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini — they're all LLMs. Different "models" = different sizes (bigger = smarter, pricier, slower) and different training data.
af-llm-basics.why:
Once you understand AI just **predicts the next word**, all your unrealistic expectations fall away. "Why did AI mess up 47×83?" — because it doesn't calculate, it guesses the next digit. "Why doesn't it remember yesterday?" — because yesterday's conversation isn't in its training data.

It's like understanding that a car isn't a horse. A horse knows the way. A car doesn't. You have to drive it.
af-llm-basics.when:
Before you seriously start using AI at work. Before arguing with a colleague about "AI should / shouldn't do X". Before estimating "how much will this cost" — cost depends on model size.

If you've worked with AI for a year — skip if you want, but check yourself: do you know **why** AI sometimes fails on simple things? If not, come back.
af-llm-basics.impact:
Before: "AI should know, it's AI after all". Surprise when it fails. Endless prompt rewrites.

After: "AI is a smart word-guesser on top of a huge text corpus. Some things it guesses brilliantly, some it gets wrong. I know which is which".

Main point: instead of fighting AI, you start using it correctly.
af-llm-basics.example:
You ask AI: "What's 47 × 83?"

AI guesses: "3901" (correct is 3901 — but AI might miss, e.g. answer "3851").

Why? It's not a calculator. It's guessing "after 47 × 83 = usually something close to ...". If this exact multiplication wasn't in the training data — you get an approximation.

**Fix:** give AI a calculator as a [[node:cap-tools|tool]] — it'll call it, get the exact answer, then tell you 3901. Not guessing, but real math.

For what Claude specifically can and cannot do, see [[node:cap-limitations|Capabilities & Limitations]].
af-llm-basics.mistakes:
Main mistake: thinking AI **knows** facts. It doesn't — it memorized word patterns. Today's news, exact numbers from your report, your colleagues' names — none of that is inside.

Second mistake: trusting AI when it sounds confident. AI always sounds confident — even when making things up (called "hallucination"). Check facts, especially numbers and dates.

af-embeddings.title: Embeddings — how AI understands "by meaning"
af-embeddings.what:
You know how Google Photos finds "all the cats" in your photos, even though you never labeled any? Or how Spotify finds "similar songs" when you play something new?

That runs on **embeddings** — every word, photo, or song gets turned into a set of numbers (a vector). Similar things get similar numbers. AI then just compares: "these two sets of numbers are close, so the meanings are close".
af-embeddings.why:
Regular search looks for **exact words**. You type "internet not working" — Google searches pages with the words "internet", "not", "working". If a page is called "WiFi problems at home" — it won't show up, even though it's about the same thing.

Embedding-based search looks **by meaning**. "Internet not working" = "WiFi problems at home" — close number sets, so it finds both.

It's the same magic that lets AI understand "forgot my password, help" and "how do I reset my password" are the same thing.
af-embeddings.when:
When you need to search large piles of documents and exact-words aren't enough. When you're building search that should "understand" what users mean. When you want recommendations "similar products / docs / customers".

Everything [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] does — stands on embeddings.
af-embeddings.impact:
Before: user asks "email not arriving", then FAQ search returns nothing (FAQ says "email delivery failures"), then customer goes to support.

After: embeddings catch "email not arriving" = "email delivery failures", then finds the FAQ, then customer self-serves.

Main point: self-service search quality jumps 2-3× without rewriting any content.
af-embeddings.example:
You have a Notion article "Password reset: step-by-step guide". An employee asks the Slack bot: "forgot my password, help".

Without embeddings: bot looks for the word "forgot" in articles. "Forgot" isn't in the title, so nothing found, so "contact admin".

With embeddings: "forgot my password, help" becomes a number set. "Password reset: guide" becomes a similar number set. Bot finds the article, then drops the link, then employee solves it in 5 seconds.

Anthropic doesn't ship its own embeddings: for hybrid architectures common choices are Voyage AI, OpenAI text-embedding-3, and open-source models.
af-embeddings.mistakes:
Main mistake: using embeddings from a random model. Old cheap model = bad number sets = bad matches. Solid options today — OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere embed, or natively in Claude.

Second mistake: thinking embeddings = "AI understands meaning like a human". It understands **pattern similarity**. Sometimes finds completely the wrong thing — especially for rare terms or in-house slang.

af-vector-db.title: Vector Database — a library for meanings
af-vector-db.what:
You know how in a library books are shelved by topic, not alphabetically? Pick up a book on gardening — 10 more on gardening sit nearby. Handy when you search by meaning.
