i-when-where.mistakes: Duplicating global rules into every Project, then not understanding why editing the global one changes nothing inside the project.

pr-constraints.title: Constraints and taboos
pr-constraints.what: An explicit list of what the model must NOT do: no preamble, no more than 5 points, do not invent numbers, do not change the format.
pr-constraints.why: A ban works more precisely than praise: "no preamble" is more reliable than "be concise". The model grasps a boundary better than a wish.
pr-constraints.when: When answers keep drifting: extra intros, filler, invented facts, wrong length or tone.
pr-constraints.impact: A couple of precise bans remove most of the typical "noise" in an answer and make the result predictable.
pr-constraints.example: Constraints: no intros or "hope this helps" lines; max 5 points; if data is missing, write "I do not know" instead of inventing.
pr-constraints.mistakes: Writing bans vaguely ("do not write badly") — the model will not get the boundary. A ban must name a specific action.

pr-antipatterns.title: Prompt anti-patterns
pr-antipatterns.what: Common request mistakes that make answers "bad": a one-liner "do it well", a wall of text with no structure, polite noise, "think step by step" where the model already reasons.
pr-antipatterns.why: You learn fastest from failures: seeing why a prompt did not work stops you repeating it.
pr-antipatterns.when: When the answer disappoints but you cannot tell why — check the anti-pattern list before blaming the model.
pr-antipatterns.impact: Removing 2-3 anti-patterns often turns the same prompt from "useless" into "working" without changing the model.
pr-antipatterns.example: Bad: "write about marketing". Good: "You are a marketer. 3 post ideas for a B2B LinkedIn audience, 2 sentences each, no hashtags".
pr-antipatterns.mistakes: Adding "this is very important" and "please try hard" — a modern model ignores this and the prompt just bloats.

cc-background-tasks.title: Background tasks
cc-background-tasks.what: Long tasks in Claude Code that keep running while you do something else: you start a command in the background, and the assistant returns to you when it finishes.
cc-background-tasks.why: Without background runs you block the chat for minutes waiting on a build or tests. A background task frees the conversation — you ask the next thing without waiting.
cc-background-tasks.when: When a command takes longer than 30 seconds (tests, build, indexing) and you do not need the result instantly.
cc-background-tasks.impact: You parallelize work: while tests run in the background, the assistant already edits the next file. On big projects that is hours saved a day.
cc-background-tasks.example: Ask: "run the full test suite in the background and keep refactoring the login module" — tests start in the background and report when done.
cc-background-tasks.mistakes: Pushing a command to the background when you need its result right now for the next step — then you are still waiting, just blindly.

cc-scheduled-runs.title: Scheduled runs
cc-scheduled-runs.what: A task that runs automatically on a clock: "every morning", "Mondays at 9:00", "hourly". The assistant starts on its own, does the work, and sends the result.
cc-scheduled-runs.why: Routine that repeats on a calendar (a digest, a release check, a summary) is silly to run by hand — you forget or run it at the wrong time.
cc-scheduled-runs.when: For time-based recurring tasks with no human in the moment: a morning digest, a nightly check, a weekly report.
cc-scheduled-runs.impact: The task runs reliably and on time even when you are away. Zero misses from the human factor.
cc-scheduled-runs.example: Set: "every Monday at 9:00 gather the week's new tasks and send a summary by priority" — the assistant starts itself.
cc-scheduled-runs.mistakes: Scheduling a task that spends paid tokens and forgetting it — over a month the bill grows for runs no one reads.

cc-hooks-blocking.title: Blocking hooks
cc-hooks-blocking.what: A hook that does not just run a command on an event but can STOP the assistant's action: forbid a dangerous call or require confirmation before writing to a protected file.
cc-hooks-blocking.why: A regular hook reacts after the fact. A blocking one is a safety catch: it stands before the action and refuses what is not allowed. More reliable than persuasion by text.
cc-hooks-blocking.when: When there are actions the assistant must not take on its own: deleting in production, publishing to the main branch, writing secrets, paid calls.
cc-hooks-blocking.impact: A guarantee, not a hope: a forbidden action physically will not run even if the model "decides" it should. Removes a whole class of incidents.
cc-hooks-blocking.example: Before a command runs, the hook checks it for dangerous patterns (mass delete, force push) — finds one, returns a block, and the action does not run.
cc-hooks-blocking.mistakes: Relying on a text instruction "never do X" instead of a blocking hook — the model can ignore an instruction, but not a hook.

ag-orchestration.title: Agent orchestration
ag-orchestration.what: Several agents working under a lead: the lead splits the task, hands pieces to specialized helpers, and assembles their results into one answer.
ag-orchestration.why: One agent with two dozen tools gets confused and overflows its context. Orchestration gives each worker a narrow role and clean context — quality goes up.
ag-orchestration.when: When a task breaks into different parts: "find, then analyze, then format", where each step is done best by a separate specialist.
ag-orchestration.impact: Complex multi-step tasks resolve predictably: the lead controls the flow, helpers do not interfere. The setup is easier to debug than one know-it-all.
ag-orchestration.example: For "prepare a market overview", the lead runs a research helper to find sources, then hands the findings to an analyst for a comparison table.
ag-orchestration.mistakes: Spawning helpers where one would do: orchestration adds latency for context handoff. Split into agents only when the roles are truly different.

ag-context-handoff.title: Context handoff between agents
ag-context-handoff.what: How one agent passes its result to another: what to send (the conclusion, not all the reasoning "noise"), in what format, and how much. A helper does not see the parent's context automatically.
ag-context-handoff.why: The most common break in agent chains is the second agent getting either too little (missing data) or too much (drowning in someone else's context and losing focus).
ag-context-handoff.when: Always when you build a chain of two or more agents: design the input/output "contract" for each handoff up front.
ag-context-handoff.impact: A clean handoff means each agent works with the minimum context it needs: faster, cheaper in tokens, fewer made-up answers from extra noise.
ag-context-handoff.example: The researcher hands the analyst not the whole search log but a structured list: "5 sources and the key fact from each" — exactly what the table needs.
ag-context-handoff.mistakes: Forwarding the whole raw output "so nothing is lost" — you bloat the context and pay for tokens that only get in the way.

auto-human-in-loop.title: Human in the loop
auto-human-in-loop.what: Points in automation where the assistant must stop and ask a human before an irreversible or costly action: apply a change, email a client, spend money.
auto-human-in-loop.why: Full autonomy is dangerous where a mistake is expensive. Human in the loop keeps the automation fast but returns control exactly at the critical points.
auto-human-in-loop.when: Before irreversible actions (deleting, publishing, paying, external communication) and when the model's confidence is low.
auto-human-in-loop.impact: Automation speed without the "did it and never asked" risk: most steps run themselves, the critical ones pass through your confirmation.
auto-human-in-loop.example: The assistant drafts a client reply entirely on its own, but before sending shows the draft "send?" — the email goes only after your yes.
auto-human-in-loop.mistakes: Putting a confirmation on every step — then automation loses its point and you click everything by hand again. Stop only at the truly risky moments.

auto-spend-limits.title: Spend limits
auto-spend-limits.what: A ceiling on autonomous work: a maximum of tokens or money per task or per period. On reaching the limit, the assistant stops and asks instead of burning more budget.
auto-spend-limits.why: An autonomous or scheduled agent in a loop can quietly spend a lot: it loops, repeats an expensive call, runs a heavy model where a light one would do.
auto-spend-limits.when: Mandatory for anything running unattended: schedules, background tasks, long autonomous agents.
auto-spend-limits.impact: A predictable bill instead of an end-of-month surprise. An agent failure costs "the limit", not "the whole budget".
auto-spend-limits.example: Give a nightly agent a limit of "no more than $2 per run": hit the ceiling and it writes "reached the limit, stopped" instead of looping on.
auto-spend-limits.mistakes: Running an autonomous agent with no spend ceiling at all, hoping "it is sensible" — one bug in a loop and the bill grows tenfold.

auto-retry-recovery.title: Retries and recovery
auto-retry-recovery.what: Behavior on a failed step: instead of stopping at once, the assistant retries with a pause, and after a few failures ends cleanly with a clear message rather than hanging.
auto-retry-recovery.why: In autonomous work, failures are inevitable: the network blinks, an external service errors, a rate limit is hit. Without retries one random error wrecks the whole task.
auto-retry-recovery.when: In any automation with external calls (network, third-party services), especially in unattended schedules and background tasks.
auto-retry-recovery.impact: Resilience: random temporary failures survive on their own, and only real problems reach a human, not "the network blinked".
auto-retry-recovery.example: The agent calls an external service, gets "temporarily unavailable" — waits a couple of seconds and tries again; after 3 failures writes "service down, deferred".
auto-retry-recovery.mistakes: Retrying with no pause and no cap on attempts — the agent floods the service. And do not retry a non-idempotent action, or you get a double charge.

auto-webhooks-triggers.title: Webhooks and triggers
auto-webhooks-triggers.what: Running not on a clock but on an event: a new request comes in, a message lands in a channel, a ticket is created, a document changes. An external system "pings" the assistant and it gets to work at once.
auto-webhooks-triggers.why: A schedule checks "did something happen" blindly and with delay. An event trigger reacts instantly and exactly when there is something to react to — no idle runs.
auto-webhooks-triggers.when: When real-time reaction to an external event matters: replying to a new ticket, handling an incoming message, checking a fresh change.
auto-webhooks-triggers.impact: A reaction in seconds instead of "hourly on a schedule", and zero empty runs — the assistant works only when an event actually occurs.
auto-webhooks-triggers.example: Set a trigger "new ticket created" — the assistant reads it immediately, drafts a reply, and calls a human, without waiting for someone to ask.
auto-webhooks-triggers.mistakes: Attaching a heavy, expensive agent to a frequent event with no spend limit — a stream of events becomes a stream of paid runs.

en-readiness-assessment.title: AI readiness assessment
en-readiness-assessment.what: A short self-check before you start: does the company have the data, processes, people, and budget for AI to pay off rather than disappoint.
en-readiness-assessment.why: Most AI failures are not about technology but about taking on the wrong task or not being ready. The check saves months and money.
en-readiness-assessment.when: Before your first serious AI project and before each big expansion, when leadership is unsure "can we handle it".
en-readiness-assessment.impact: It filters out doomed ideas early. It turns a vague "let us adopt AI" into a list of 2-3 ready tasks.
en-readiness-assessment.example: A 5-question checklist: the task repeats dozens of times a week; data is in one place; the AI answer can be verified; someone will own it; we can survive a mistake. Three "yes" — pilot it.
en-readiness-assessment.mistakes: Starting with the company's hardest, most important task — that is where the cost of a mistake is highest. Test readiness on a small, safe process.

en-adoption-roadmap.title: Step-by-step AI adoption
en-adoption-roadmap.what: A clear sequence: where to begin, what to do next, and how not to skip a stage when rolling AI out in a company.
en-adoption-roadmap.why: Companies either stall in endless discussion or want "AI everywhere" at once. Both fail. A step path gives rhythm and quick wins.
en-adoption-roadmap.when: Right after the readiness check, once the decision to adopt is made but the order of actions is unclear.
en-adoption-roadmap.impact: A first visible result in a couple of weeks instead of half a year. It lowers team resistance — people see value on a small example.
en-adoption-roadmap.example: Step 1: one pilot task for 1-2 people. Step 2: measure the time saved. Step 3: write a simple how-to. Step 4: expand to the team. Step 5: the next task.
en-adoption-roadmap.mistakes: Launching five directions at once — attention scatters and none reaches a result. One pilot to a win, then the next.

uc-ai-customer-assistant.title: AI assistant for customers
uc-ai-customer-assistant.what: A path to launching an AI that advises customers on your products, services, and terms right on the site or in a messenger.
uc-ai-customer-assistant.why: Customers ask the same questions and leave when no answer comes. A live agent is expensive and does not work at night.
uc-ai-customer-assistant.when: When the flow of identical questions is large and a knowledge base (prices, terms, answers) already exists in some form.
uc-ai-customer-assistant.impact: Most routine questions are handled without a human. Staff step in only for the hard cases.
uc-ai-customer-assistant.example: An electronics shop: the AI answers "is this laptop good for video editing", checking specs from the catalog, and suggests 2-3 models in budget.
uc-ai-customer-assistant.mistakes: Launching without testing on real questions — the AI will confidently invent delivery and warranty terms. Test on fifty typical questions first.
